slides.title: Welcome to JEE Chemistry (Mechanics)
slides.content:
# JEE Main Chemistry: Mechanics Focus

Welcome to this unique module!

*(Note: According to the syllabus mapping, this section specifically tests rigorous physical mechanics calculations)*

## What You Will Learn:
- **Kinematics problems** - Describing motion mathematically
- **Dynamics applications** - Forces and acceleration
- **Work-energy theorem** - The alternate way to solve
- **Rotational motion** - Spinning objects
- **Gravitation calculations** - Planets and orbits

slides.title: Kinematics Problems
slides.content:
# Kinematics: The Language of Motion

Kinematics does not care *why* an object is moving. It only cares about *how* it is moving.

We use three primary variables:
1. **Displacement:** Where is it? (Vector)
2. **Velocity:** How fast is its position changing? (Vector)
3. **Acceleration:** How fast is its velocity changing? (Vector)

slides.title: Equations of Motion
slides.content:
# The Big Three Equations

If acceleration is constant, all kinematic problems can be solved using three equations.

1. Final velocity equals initial velocity plus acceleration times time.
2. Displacement equals initial velocity times time plus one-half acceleration times time squared.
3. Final velocity squared equals initial velocity squared plus two times acceleration times displacement.

Mastering when to use which equation is the key to speed in the JEE exam.

slides.title: Projectile Motion
slides.content:
# 2D Kinematics

When a ball is thrown in the air, it moves in two dimensions simultaneously.

## The Secret Trick:
Gravity ONLY pulls down. It does not pull sideways.

Therefore, you completely separate the X (horizontal) and Y (vertical) math. The horizontal velocity never changes (zero acceleration), while the vertical velocity constantly changes due to gravity. The only variable they share is Time!

slides.title: Dynamics Applications
slides.content:
# Dynamics: Why Things Move

Dynamics introduces **Mass** and **Force** into the equations.

While kinematics describes the flight of the ball, dynamics explains the force of the hand that threw it, and the friction of the air slowing it down.

slides.title: Projectile Quiz
slides.quizQuestion: In ideal projectile motion (ignoring air resistance), what happens to the horizontal component of the velocity during the flight?
quizOptions: It constantly decreases until it hits the ground
It constantly increases due to gravity
It remains perfectly constant throughout the entire flight
It drops to zero at the highest point of the arc

slides.title: Friction
slides.content:
# The Force of Friction

Friction is the force that opposes sliding motion between two surfaces.

## Static vs Kinetic:
- **Static Friction:** The force required to get a stationary object to *start* moving. It is always stronger.
- **Kinetic Friction:** The force required to *keep* an object moving. It is always weaker.

It takes more force to break a heavy box loose than it does to keep it sliding across the floor.

slides.title: Work-Energy Theorem
slides.content:
# The Work-Energy Theorem

This is one of the most powerful theorems in physics.

**The total Work done by all forces on an object exactly equals the change in its Kinetic Energy.**

If you push a block (doing positive work) and friction resists it (doing negative work), you add them together. The net work perfectly predicts how much faster the block is now moving!

slides.title: Potential Energy
slides.content:
# Storing Energy

Work done against a "conservative force" (like gravity or a spring) is not lost; it is stored as Potential Energy.

If you lift a book onto a high shelf, you did work against gravity. That energy is now stored in the book's height. If the book falls, gravity does work, converting that stored potential energy back into kinetic energy (speed).

slides.title: Rotational Motion
slides.content:
# Spinning Objects

Everything you learned in linear mechanics translates perfectly to rotational mechanics.

- Linear Mass becomes **Moment of Inertia** (how hard it is to start spinning).
- Linear Force becomes **Torque** (twisting force).
- Linear Momentum becomes **Angular Momentum**.

slides.title: Moment of Inertia
slides.content:
# The Resistance to Spin

Moment of Inertia depends not just on how much mass an object has, but *where* that mass is located.

Mass located far away from the axis of rotation is much harder to spin than mass located close to the center.

This is why a tightrope walker carries a long, heavy pole. The massive pole has a huge moment of inertia, making it very difficult for the walker to accidentally tip over and spin off the rope!

slides.title: Rotation Quiz
slides.content: Verify your understanding of spinning objects.
slides.quizQuestion: Why does an ice skater spin much faster when they pull their arms in close to their body?
quizOptions: Because pulling their arms in decreases their Moment of Inertia, and to conserve angular momentum, their spin speed must increase
Because pulling their arms in increases their friction with the ice

slides.title: Torque and Equilibrium
slides.content:
# Twisting Forces

**Torque** is defined as Force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the pivot point (the lever arm).

If you want to open a heavy door, you push on the handle (far from the hinges) because the large distance creates a massive Torque. If you push right next to the hinges, the distance is tiny, so the Torque is tiny, and the door won't move.

slides.title: Gravitation Calculations
slides.content:
# Newton's Law of Gravitation

Newton realized that the force making an apple fall is the exact same force keeping the Moon in orbit.

Every object in the universe attracts every other object. The force is proportional to their masses, and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.

If you double the distance between two planets, the gravitational force between them drops to one-quarter!

slides.title: Orbital Velocity
slides.content:
# Falling Around the Earth

An orbit is simply falling forever.

If you throw a ball, it falls to the ground. If you fire it out of a massive cannon, it goes further before hitting the ground.

If you fire it fast enough (Orbital Velocity), the Earth curves away underneath the ball at the exact same rate the ball is falling. The ball never hits the ground; it is in orbit!

slides.title: Escape Velocity
slides.content:
# Leaving the Planet

If you throw an object up, gravity pulls it back down. 

However, gravity gets weaker the further away you get. If you throw a rocket incredibly fast (Escape Velocity), it will travel so far, so quickly, that gravity weakens to near zero before it can pull the rocket back.

The rocket permanently escapes the planet's gravitational well.

slides.title: Summary of Mechanics Applications
slides.content:
# Mechanics Summary

## Key Takeaways:
- **Kinematics** separates 2D motion into independent X and Y components.
- **Dynamics** relies on forces, including the difference between Static and Kinetic friction.
- The **Work-Energy Theorem** provides a shortcut to solving problems without calculating acceleration.
- **Rotational Motion** introduces Moment of Inertia and Torque, following the strict conservation of Angular Momentum.
- **Gravitation** dictates orbits (falling forever) and Escape Velocity (breaking the gravitational pull entirely).
